Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

A sales forecast is a prediction of future sales revenue based on historical data, industry trends, and the status of the current sales pipeline. Businesses use the sales forecast to estimate weekly, monthly, quarterly, and annual sales totals. A company needs to make an accurate sales forecast as it adds value across an organization and helps the different verticals to chalk out their future course of action.

Forecasting helps an organization plan its sales operations by region and provides valuable insights to the supply chain team regarding the procurement of goods and materials. An accurate sales forecast process has many benefits which include improved decision-making about the future and reduction of sales pipeline and forecast risks. Moreover, it helps to reduce the time spent in planning territory coverage and establish benchmarks that can be used to assess trends in the future.

Objective¶

SuperKart is a retail chain operating supermarkets and food marts across various tier cities, offering a wide range of products. To optimize its inventory management and make informed decisions around regional sales strategies, SuperKart wants to accurately forecast the sales revenue of its outlets for the upcoming quarter.

To operationalize these insights at scale, the company has partnered with a data science firm—not just to build a predictive model based on historical sales data, but to develop and deploy a robust forecasting solution that can be integrated into SuperKart’s decision-making systems and used across its network of stores.

Data Description¶

The data contains the different attributes of the various products and stores.The detailed data dictionary is given below.

  • Product_Id - unique identifier of each product, each identifier having two letters at the beginning followed by a number.
  • Product_Weight - weight of each product
  • Product_Sugar_Content - sugar content of each product like low sugar, regular and no sugar
  • Product_Allocated_Area - ratio of the allocated display area of each product to the total display area of all the products in a store
  • Product_Type - broad category for each product like meat, snack foods, hard drinks, dairy, canned, soft drinks, health and hygiene, baking goods, bread, breakfast, frozen foods, fruits and vegetables, household, seafood, starchy foods, others
  • Product_MRP - maximum retail price of each product
  • Store_Id - unique identifier of each store
  • Store_Establishment_Year - year in which the store was established
  • Store_Size - size of the store depending on sq. feet like high, medium and low
  • Store_Location_City_Type - type of city in which the store is located like Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3. Tier 1 consists of cities where the standard of living is comparatively higher than its Tier 2 and Tier 3 counterparts.
  • Store_Type - type of store depending on the products that are being sold there like Departmental Store, Supermarket Type 1, Supermarket Type 2 and Food Mart
  • Product_Store_Sales_Total - total revenue generated by the sale of that particular product in that particular store

Dataset Observations¶

  • The dataset has 8763 rows and 12 columns
  • We find 4 columns of float64 type, 1 column of int64 type and 7 columns of object type.
  • There are no duplicate or missing values in the dataset.

Product Observations¶

  • Product_Weight:
    • The average product weight is 12.65, with weights ranging from 4 to 22.
    • The distribution is relatively tight, with a standard deviation of ~2.22, suggesting most products are close in weight.
  • Product_Sugar_Content:
    • There are 4 distinct sugar content levels - 'Low Sugar' 'No Sugar' 'Regular' 'reg'.
    • We may have to combine 'Regular' and 'reg' later.
    • The most frequent label is "Low Sugar", making up over half the products
    (4,885 out of 8,763)
  • Product_Allocated_Area:
    • Values range from 0.004 to 0.298, with a mean of 0.069.
    • Most products occupy less than 0.1 units
  • Product_Type:
    • The data includes 16 different product types.
    • The most common type is "Fruits and Vegetables", accounting for 1,249 entries (~14%).
  • Product_MRP (Maximum Retail Price):
    • Product prices vary from 31 to 266, with an average price of 147.03.
    • This wide range suggests inclusion of both budget and premium products.

Store Observations¶

  • Store_Id:
    • There are 4 unique stores in the dataset.
    • One store (OUT004) accounts for more than 53% of the entries, suggesting it either stocks the widest range of products or has the highest reporting frequency.
  • Store_Establishment_Year:
    • Stores were established in the following years 2009, 1999, 1987, 1998.
    • Most stores are relatively modern (75th percentile is 2009).
  • Store_Size:
    • Stores are classified into three size categories: High, Medium, and Low.
    • The majority of stores are "Medium" sized (6,025 out of 8,763), indicating mid-sized retail stores dominate the dataset.
  • Store_Location_City_Type:
    • Stores are located in Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 cities, based on standard of living.
    • The majority (72%) are in Tier 2 cities, suggesting the dataset is largely representative of mid-level urban markets.
  • Store_Type:
    • There are 4 types of stores: Departmental Store, Supermarket Type 1 & 2, and Food Mart.
    • Supermarket Type 2 is the most common (appearing in 4,676 rows), possibly indicating a preferred retail format for a large number of products.
  • Product_Store_Sales_Total:
    • Sales range from 33 to 8,000, with an average of 3,464 and a standard deviation of 1,066.
    • The broad spread in sales indicates diverse product performances, likely influenced by factors like product type, price, store size, and location.

Key Observations:¶

  • The dataset offers a rich blend of product diversity and store-level context, allowing for detailed market and operational analysis.
  • Fruits and Vegetables, Low Sugar products, and mid-range prices dominate the product space.
  • Most data is concentrated in medium-sized, Tier 2 city stores, particularly in Supermarket Type 2 formats.
  • Sales data exhibits high variability, indicating opportunities for product optimization and store-specific marketing strategies.

Univariate Analysis¶

In [ ]:
#Function to plot both histogram and boxplot

def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(15, 10), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (15,10))
    kde: whether to show the density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a triangle will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=True, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=True, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram

    # Calculate and plot mean and median only if the feature is numeric
    if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[feature]):
      ax_hist2.axvline(
          data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
      )  # Add mean to the histogram
      ax_hist2.axvline(
          data[feature].median(), color="blue", linestyle="-"
      )  # Add median to the histogram
    else:
      #add mode
      ax_hist2.axvline(
          data[feature].mode()[0], color="blue", linestyle="-"
      )
In [ ]:
# function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 2, 6))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 2, 6))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        palette="Paired",
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n],
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot

Product_Type¶

In [ ]:
labeled_barplot(data, 'Product_Type', perc=True)

Insights

  • Fruits and Vegetables is the most prevalent product type with a count of 1,249 (14.3%).

  • Snack Foods follows very closely as the second most common category with 1,149 items (13.1%).

  • These two categories are clear leaders and represent a significant portion of the total product count, suggesting they are core categories for this business or dataset.

  • Following the top two, there is a group of categories with substantial counts, ranging from approximately 600 to 800 items. These include:

    • Frozen Foods: 811
    • Dairy: 796
    • Household: 740
    • Baking Goods: 716
    • Canned: 677
    • Health and Hygiene: 628
    • Meat: 618
    • This tier represents the bulk of the remaining core product offerings.

  • There is a noticeable drop-off in frequency after the "Meat" category.

  • Soft Drinks stands alone with a count of 519.

  • The remaining categories have significantly lower counts (200 or less), suggesting they are either less-stocked or more specialized/niche product types. These include:

    • Breads (200)
    • Hard Drinks (186)
    • Others (151)
    • Starchy Foods (141)
    • Breakfast (106)
    • Seafood is the least frequent category with only 76 items.

  • The high counts in categories like "Fruits and Vegetables" and "Snack Foods" imply that these products likely require the most significant inventory and

prominent shelf space in a retail environment.

  • These top categories are likely key drivers of foot traffic and sales. Marketing efforts, promotions, and cross-selling strategies could be heavily focused on these popular product types.
  • The distribution shows a strong focus on essential food items (produce, snacks, dairy, frozen) and household goods. The lower counts in categories like "Seafood" or "Breakfast" could represent an opportunity for expansion or may be a deliberate strategy to focus on higher-turnover items.
  • The "Others" category is relatively small (151 items). It indicates that most products have been successfully classified into meaningful categories.

  • This distribution also shows an imbalance. The number of medium sized stores are greater than three times the number of high-sized stores and more than five times the number of small-sized stores.
  • The business's strategy could be to focus on medium sized stores.
  • We probably should later focus on F1-score, Precision-Recall and not only on accuracy metrics.

Store_Location_City_Type¶

In [ ]:
labeled_barplot(data, 'Store_Location_City_Type', perc=True)

Insights

  • We see the dominance of Tier 2 cities (71.5%) from the graph and also the imbalance it depicts.
  • Data from the Tier 2 cities are nearly five times greater than those of Tier 1 and Tier 3 cities.
  • Similar to Store_Size, we probably should later focus on F1-score, Precision-Recall and not only on accuracy metrics.

Store_Type¶

In [ ]:
labeled_barplot(data, 'Store_Type', perc=True)

Insights

  • Supermarket Type2 is the dominant category here and accounts for 53.4%. This means more than half the data points fall under this single store type.
  • The business structure could be to have Type2 super markets.
  • The remaining three categories have smaller shares:
    • Supermarket Type1: 18.1%
    • Departmental Store: 15.4%
    • Food Mart: 13.1%
  • Once again, the dataset is seen to be imbalanced.
  • As before, it will be important to use evaluation metrics that are robust to class imbalance: F1-score, Precision, Recall to get a true sense of the performance across all store types.
  • We might have to resort to using stratified sampling or using SMOTE to oversample minority class.

Bivariate Analysis¶

Correlation matrix¶

In [ ]:
# plot correlation on numeric columns
corr =  data.select_dtypes(include=['number']).corr()

plt.figure(figsize=(6,4))

sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, vmin=-1, vmax=1, fmt=".2f", cmap="Spectral")

plt.title("Correlation Heatmap")
plt.show()

Insights

  • We can observe few key relationships regarding what drives Product_Store_Sales_Total.
  • Strongest Positive Correlations:
    • Product_MRP and Product_Store_Sales_Total (Correlation: 0.79): This is the strongest relationship on the map. The dark teal color highlights it visually.
    This is logical as more expensive products generate higher sales revenue.
    • Product_Weight and Product_Store_Sales_Total (Correlation: 0.74): This is another strong positive correlation. This might be because heavier items are often bulk goods or more substantial products that naturally have a higher price point.
    • Product_Weight and Product_MRP (Correlation: 0.53): This is a moderate positive correlation. Heavier products tend to have a higher MRP, suggesting that weight and price are linked, and both contribute to higher sales.
  • Product_MRP and Product_Weight could be very strong predictors of sales. We should also note that Product_MRP and Product_Weight also demonstrate multicollinearity as they are moderately correlated. Hopefully this is not high enough to cause issues.
  • Interestingly, Product_Allocated_Area has no meaningful impact on sales and this could be counter intuitive.

Distribution of Product_Weight vs Product_Store_Sales_Total¶

In [ ]:
# Scatter plot with regression line and histogram
plt.figure(figsize=[6, 4])
#sns.regplot(x=data.Product_Weight, y=data.Product_Store_Sales_Total,
#            scatter_kws={'color': 'purple', 'alpha': 0.5},
#            line_kws={'color': 'Green'})

sns.jointplot(x=data.Product_Weight, y=data.Product_Store_Sales_Total, kind='reg',
            scatter_kws={'color': 'purple', 'alpha': 0.5},
            line_kws={'color': 'Green'})

plt.show()

<Figure size 600x400 with 0 Axes>

Insights

  • Positive Correlation: The cloud of purple data points clearly trends upwards from the bottom-left to the top-right. This visually confirms that as Product_Weight increases, Product_Store_Sales_Total also tends to increase.
  • The linear regression line cuts through the center of the data cloud, indicating that the relationship between the weight and sales is linear.
  • While some significant scatter is observed, the points are tight around the linear regression line. This is consistent with the 0.74 correlation seen in the heatmap.
  • While the general rule "heavier means more sales" holds true, the increasing variability for heavier items suggests that other factors (like brand, category, or promotions) could be playing a role in determining the final sales for these larger products.

Distribution of Product_Allocated_Area vs Product_Store_Sales_Total¶

In [ ]:
# Scatter plot with regression line and histogram
plt.figure(figsize=[6, 4])

sns.jointplot(x=data.Product_Allocated_Area, y=data.Product_Store_Sales_Total, kind='reg',
            scatter_kws={'color': 'purple', 'alpha': 0.5},
            line_kws={'color': 'Green'})

plt.show()

<Figure size 600x400 with 0 Axes>

Insights

  • The correlation heatmap previously suggested no meaningful linear relationship between Product_Allocated_Area and Product_Store_Sales_Total. This is confirmed by the above plot.
  • The purple data points form a shapeless, and somewhat rectangular cloud with no upward or downward trend. The points are widely scattered across the entire range of sales values, regardless of the allocated area.
  • The solid green regression line is almost perfectly flat (horizontal). A horizontal line means that as the value on the x-axis (Product_Allocated_Area) increases, the predicted value on the y-axis (Product_Store_Sales_Total) does not change. This is the textbook graphical representation of a zero correlation.
  • The data points are heavily concentrated on the left side of the plot, where the Product_Allocated_Area is low. As you move to the right (larger allocated area), the data points become much sparser.
  • This is a very important insight for retail and category management. It suggests that strategies like "giving a product a bigger display to boost its sales" may be ineffective. The decision to allocate more space should likely be based on other factors, such as a product's existing high performance, promotional activities, or strategic importance, rather than being used as a tool to force high performance.
  • Product_Allocated_Area would probably be a very poor feature to model predicted sales and could be considered for removal from the model without sacrificing accuracy.

Distribution of Product_MRP vs Product_Store_Sales_Total¶

In [ ]:
# Scatter plot with regression line and histogram
plt.figure(figsize=[6, 4])

sns.jointplot(x=data.Product_MRP, y=data.Product_Store_Sales_Total, kind='reg',
            scatter_kws={'color': 'purple', 'alpha': 0.5},
            line_kws={'color': 'Green'})

plt.show()

<Figure size 600x400 with 0 Axes>

Insights

  • We saw the MRP and Sales had a strong correlation (0.79) in the heatmap and hence was the primary driver of sales revenue.
  • The above plot confirms this - The purple data points form a tight, distinct, upward-sloping band. This is a classic visual representation of a strong positive correlation—as Product_MRP (x-axis) increases, Product_Store_Sales_Total (y-axis) increases with it.
  • The green linear regression line cuts through the data cloud indicating a predominantly linear relationship.
  • The data points seem to be grouped in the following bands (instead of being uniformly scattered):
    • 50-100
    • 100-150
    • 150-200
    • 200-250
  • These might be clustere into specific pricing tiers - Low Cost, Standard, Premium, High-end.
  • Product_MRP is seen to be an important feature for an machine learning model aiming to predict sales. A simple linear regression model using MRP as a feature would likely perform very well. The distinct bands suggest that a model might even benefit from treating price as a categorical feature (e.g., "Price Tier 1," "Price Tier 2," etc.) in addition to its numerical value.

Insights

  • The above table and barplots, show clearly which product categories are the most and least significant contributors to the store's total revenue.

  • We can probably categorize them into:

    • Tier 1 (generating revenue > 3.5 Million)
      • Fruits & Vegetables, Snack Foods
      • Responsible for a huge portion of total sales. These also had the highest product counts. There might be a strong correlation between product variety/volume and total sales.
    • Tier 2 (generating revenue between 2 Million - 3 Million)
      • Dairy, Frozen Foods, Household, Baking Goods, Canned,Health and Hygiene,Meat.
      • This is a broad and significant tier.
      • The sales figures are very close for "Dairy" and "Frozen Foods," making them equally important.
      • "Household" and "Health and Hygiene" also demonstrate that non-food items are very significant revenue drivers.
    • Tier 3 (Mid-level revenue less than 2 Million)
      • Soft drinks sits in its own tier.
      • We saw that it had relatively high product count but sales are lower than food and household categories.
    • Tier 4 (Miscellaneous with revenue less than 1 Million)
      • Breads, Hard Drinks, Others, Starchy Foods, Breakfast, Seafood
      • Seafood was the lowest-performing category at 272k.

  • Business Implications

    • Resource Allocation: Marketing budgets, promotional activities, and prime shelf space (like end caps and front-of-store displays) should be heavily focused on the Tier 1 and Tier 2 categories to maximize returns.
    • Growth Opportunities: Categories in Tier 3 and Tier 4 could be analyzed for growth potential.
    • Profitability Analysis: While this chart shows revenue, the next step would be to analyze profitability (sales minus cost of goods sold). A high-revenue category like "Snack Foods" might have lower profit margins than a smaller category like "Health and Hygiene."

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))

plt.xticks(rotation=90)

plt.ylabel('Product_Store_Sales_Total')
plt.title('Product_Sugar_Content vs Product_Store_Sales_Total')
plt.show()

Insights

  • We saw in previously that "Low Sugar" was the most numerous product type. This chart confirms it and also translates directly into highest sales revenue.

  • The "Regular" and "reg" data inconsistency is also reflected here and probably should be combined.

  • "Low Sugar" products generated over 16.8 million in sales, which is more than the combined sales of all other categories.

  • There is a distinct hierarchy in revenue generation based on sugar content:

    • Low Sugar: 16.82 million
    • Regular: 7.87 million
    • No Sugar: 5.27 million
    • reg: 0.39 million (approximately 394k)

  • "Low Sugar" products sell more than double the amount of "Regular" products.

  • "Regular" products, in turn, sell significantly more than "No Sugar" products.

  • The "reg" category is almost negligible in terms of sales revenue compared to the others.

  • Business Implications

    • Market Trend: The data strongly suggests a powerful market trend towards "Low Sugar" options. Consumers are not only presented with more low-sugar choices, but they are also spending the most money on them. This indicates high demand for healthier or "diet" alternatives.
    • Strategic Alignment: The company's product assortment, which is heavily skewed towards "Low Sugar" items, is perfectly aligned with consumer spending patterns. This is a sign of a successful strategy that meets market demand.
    • Revenue Focus: From a revenue perspective, the "Low Sugar" product segment is the most critical to the business. Marketing campaigns, promotions, and new product development should likely continue to focus on this lucrative category.
    • Data Cleaning: The "reg" category continues to be a minor but persistent data quality issue that should be addressed by mapping it to "Regular" for all future analyses.

  • OUT004 is not just a busy store but also the highest grossing store by a large margin compared to others.

  • We can once again categorize the stores into three categories based on sales:

    • Tier 1: OUT004
    • Tier 2: OUT003 & OUT001
    • Tier 3: OUT002

  • Business Implications

    • Store Strategy: The company is effectively running two different business models: the massive-scale operation at OUT004 and the more standard supermarket format at the other three locations. Strategies and performance metrics cannot be one-size-fits-all.

Insights

  • The plot reveals a huge disparity in sales performance, with one city tier massively outperforming the others.

  • Tier 2 locations are the undisputed revenue powerhouse, generating over 21.6 million in sales. This is more than triple the sales of Tier 1 cities and over ten times the sales of Tier 3 cities.

  • Tier 1 locations form the middle tier, with a respectable 6.67 million in total sales. While this is significantly lower than Tier 2, it is still a substantial amount of revenue.

  • Tier 3 locations contribute the least to total sales, bringing in just over 2.0 million

  • There is data imbalance with Tier 2 city having the most records.

  • Business Implications

    • Geographic Strategy: The company's business is overwhelmingly concentrated in Tier 2 cities. Their success in these cities is the primary driver of the company's overall revenue.
    • Market Potential: The lower sales in Tier 1 and Tier 3 could represent untapped market potential and hence an improvement opportunity.
    • Risk Concentration: The heavy reliance on Tier 2 cities for revenue represents a concentration risk. Any negative shifts specifically affecting Tier 2 cities would have a disproportionately large impact on the company's bottom line. It may be wise to diversify among the tiers.

    • Profitability Analysis: The next logical step would be to analyze the profitability of each format. While "Supermarket Type2" has the highest sales, it may also have the highest operating costs. The smaller "Food Mart" might have a higher profit margin even if its total profit is lower.

Distribution of Store_ID vs Product_Store_Sales_Total¶

In [ ]:
#Boxplot Store_Id vs Product_Store_Sales_Total
plt.figure(figsize=[6, 4])

sns.boxplot(data=data, x="Store_Id", y="Product_Store_Sales_Total", hue="Store_Id")
plt.xticks(rotation=90)
plt.title("Distribution of Store_Id vs Product_Store_Sales_Total")
plt.xlabel("Store_Id")
plt.ylabel("Product_Store_Sales_Total")

plt.show()

Insights

  • OUT003:
    • Highest median sales: A typical product sold at this store has the highest sale value.
    • This store sells both high and low revenue items and the average is very high.
    • Has a few outliers - maybe indicating some very successful products
  • OUT001:
    • Second highest median sales.
    • Very wide distribution: Probably sells very low revenue to very high revenue items.
    • No outliers are depicted in the graph.
  • OUT004:
    • Third highest median sales.
    • Tight distribution: Sales are consistent and predictable.
    • Large cluster of outliers observed above and below the main distribution.
  • OUT002:
    • Lowest median sales
    • Tight distribution similar to OUT004.
    • Many low end outliers - emphasizing low-priced, quick purchase items.

Business Insights:

  • OUT003 is the best store for high per-item revenue, while OUT004 is the best for high total volume.
  • The outliers at OUT004 and OUT002 suggest these stores have a core range of products with very consistent sales, and anything outside that range is an exception. In contrast, the wider distributions at OUT001 and OUT003 suggest that a broad range of sales performance is normal for them.
  • The four stores probably operate on different business models.

Distribution of Store_Size vs Product_Store_Sales_Total¶

In [ ]:
#Boxplot Store_Size vs Product_Store_Sales_Total

Insights

  • The plot reveals an unexpected observation - The "High" sized stores have highest average product sales. This is followed by "Medium" sized and "Small" sized stores.

  • Previously, we had noticed that "Medium" sized stores were dominant in total sales.

  • "High" sized stores:

    • The median is the highest (greater than 4000)
    • The distribution is wide and probably indicates sales of low to high revenue products.
    • No outliers are noticed

  • "Medium" sized stores:

    • The median is the second highest (greater than 3000)
    • Outliers are noticed at both the top and bottom (especially the top).
    • While the "Medium" size category has the highest total sales, on a per-product basis, the typical sale in a "Medium" store is lower than in a "High" store.

  • "Small" Sized stores:

    • The median is the lowest (less than 2000)
    • The distribution is compact.
    • We notice a cluster of outliers towards the low-end.

  • Business Insights:

    • Total Sales vs. Per-Item Sales: This chart provides the critical distinction between total revenue and per-item revenue.
      • "Medium" stores win on TOTAL sales (due to high volume).
      • "High" stores win on PER-ITEM sales (due to higher-value products).

Product_Sugar_Content vs Product_Type Analysis¶

In [ ]:
#Plot a heatmap of Product_Sugar_Content vs Product_Type Analysis
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.heatmap(
    pd.crosstab(data["Product_Sugar_Content"], data["Product_Type"]),
    annot=True,
    fmt="g",
    cmap="coolwarm",
)
plt.ylabel("Product_Sugar_Content")
plt.xlabel("Product_Type")
plt.title("Product_Sugar_Content vs Product_Type Analysis")
plt.show()

Insights

  • "No Sugar" category is limited to "Health and Hygiene", "Household" and "Others". The remaining values are almost all zeros. This indicates a "Niche" category.

  • "Low Sugar" dominates the following categories:

    • Fruits and Vegetables (864): Has the highest count in the heatmap.
    • Snack Foods (804)
    • Dairy (590)
    • Frozen Foods (531)
    • Baking Goods (462)
    • The high count for "Fruits and Vegetables" is interesting and might reflect how natural sugars are classified or could be a mistake in data labeling.

  • "Regular" has high numbers in "Fruits and Vegetables", "Snack Foods", "Frozen Foods" and "Dairy".

  • "reg" has very low numbers across the board. It has a distribution like the "Regular" row but with much smaller counts.

  • Business Insights:

    • Labeling: The company extensively uses the "Low Sugar" label, especially for key food categories like Snacks, Dairy, and Produce, likely to appeal to health-conscious consumers.
    • Category-Specific Sugar Content: Sugar content is not a universal attribute. It is highly relevant for food items but not for non-food items like "Household" and "Health and Hygiene," where the "No Sugar" label acts as a placeholder.
    • Dual Offerings: For major categories like Snack Foods, Fruits/Veggies, and Dairy, the company offers both "Regular" and "Low Sugar" options, indicating a strategy to capture both traditional and health-focused market segments.

  • The analysis confirms a minor data issue with the "reg" label that should be cleaned for any modeling or formal reporting.

Store_Id vs Product_Type Analysis¶

In [ ]:
#Plot a heatmap of Store_Id vs Product_Type
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.heatmap(
    pd.crosstab(data["Store_Id"], data["Product_Type"]),
    annot=True,
    fmt="g",
    cmap="coolwarm",
)
plt.ylabel("Store_Id")
plt.xlabel("Product_Type")
plt.title("Store_Id vs Product_Type Analysis")
plt.show()

Insights

  • OUT004 stands out in this plot immediately. It not only has more products overall, it also has larger assortment in each category.

  • OUT001, OUT002 and OUT003 have smaller but similar product assortments.

  • OUT004:

    • is consistently colored in oranges and reds, indicating much higher product counts across the board.
    • aims to be a one-stop shop by offering deep variety in every product category. Its massive sales (seen in previous charts) are a direct result of this enormous product selection.

  • OUT001, OUT002, OUT003 are visually very similar, dominated by shades of blue.

    • They probably carry a curated selection of products rather than the exhaustive assortment seen at OUT004.
    • OUT001 has a slightly higher count of Snack Foods (202) and Fruits and Vegetables (199) compared to the other two.
    • OUT003 has a slightly stronger showing in Fruits and Vegetables (182) and Snack Foods (186).

  • Business Insights

    • Two-Tiered Store Strategy: The company is effectively running two different types of businesses:
      • The OUT004 Model: A large-format, high-variety, one-stop-shop destination.
      • The Standard Supermarket Model: A network of smaller-format stores (OUT001, OUT002, OUT003) with a more limited but still comprehensive product range.
    • Category Management: The focus on Fruits and Vegetables and Snack Foods is a company-wide strategy, as these categories have high counts even in the smaller stores. However, the depth of this focus is what sets OUT004 apart.
    • Performance Benchmarking: This chart reinforces that it would be inappropriate to directly compare the performance of OUT004 with the other stores without accounting for the massive difference in their product assortments. The three smaller stores should be benchmarked against each other.

Product_MRP vs Product_Type Analysis¶

In [ ]:
#Plot a boxplot of Product_MRP vs Product_Type
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.boxplot(data=data, x="Product_Type", y="Product_MRP", hue="Product_Type")
plt.xticks(rotation=90)
plt.ylabel("Product_MRP")
plt.xlabel("Product_Type")
plt.title("Product_MRP vs Product_Type Analysis")
plt.show()

Insights

  • Median price for almost all categories are in the 140-150 range.

  • The company probably uses a standardized, tiered pricing strategy that is applied broadly across its product portfolio.

  • Few categories have slightly different pricing profiles:

    • "Starchy Foods" and "Others" appear to have a slightly higher median price
    • "Canned" has a slightly lower median price compared to its immediate neighbors.

  • Outliers are noticed on the low end and also the high end in many categories.

  • Business Insights:

    • Portfolio-Wide Pricing Strategy: The company applies a consistent, tiered pricing architecture across its entire range of products. This simplifies pricing management and creates a predictable price perception for customers.
    • Margin Management: This strategy suggests that profit margins might vary significantly between categories. If a high-cost category like "Meat" is subject to the same pricing structure as a lower-cost category like "Snack Foods," their profitability profiles will be very different.
    • Each category contains a mix of products that fit into the company's predefined low, standard, and premium price tiers.

Product_MRP vs Store_Id Analysis¶

In [ ]:
#Boxplot of Product_MRP vs Store_Id
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.boxplot(data=data, x="Store_Id", y="Product_MRP", hue="Store_Id")
plt.xticks(rotation=90)
plt.ylabel("Product_MRP")
plt.xlabel("Store_Id")
plt.title("Product_MRP vs Store_Id Analysis")
plt.show()

Insights

  • It is seen from the plot that all stores do not carry the same mix of products in terms of price.

  • OUT003 appears to focus on higher-priced goods, while OUT002 focuses on lower-priced goods. OUT001 and OUT004 carry a more balanced, full range of products.

  • OUT003:

    • The median MRP is the highest of all four stores (around 175).
    • The outliers indicate that though, the store is focused on premium priced products, it does carry low priced items.

  • OUT001:

    • The median MRP is the second highest (around 165)
    • This store has the tallest box and hence few outliers.
    • Probably carries everything from a low priced item to premium priced goods.

  • OUT004:

    • The median MRP is right in the middle of the overall price distribution, around 140.
    • The box is centered and symmetrical, indicating a balanced mix of products from the lower and upper price tiers.
    • Similar to OUT001, it carries a wide range of products, and hence fewer outliers.

  • OUT002:

    • The median MRP is by far the lowest, sitting at just over 100.
    • The entire box is shifted downwards and is probably due to focus on products cheaper than the remaining stores.
    • The cluster of outliers at the top indicates that it does carry some higher-priced goods.

  • Business Insights:

    • Diverse Pricing Strategies: The company employs different pricing and assortment strategies for its different stores, tailoring them to specific formats or markets.
    • Connecting to Sales Performance: The pricing strategy directly impacts sales performance. The low prices at OUT002 lead to lower per-item sales and lower total sales. The high prices at OUT003 lead to high per-item sales. The balanced, high-volume approach at OUT004 leads to the highest total sales overall. This analysis provides a deep understanding of the business model of each individual store.

EDA Insights

  • The exploratory data analysis of the SuperKart dataset reveals several crucial insights for building a predictive model for product sales.

  • The target variable, Product_Sales, is skewed, which might require transformation for some modeling techniques.

  • Key drivers of sales appear to be Product_Price and Store_Type.

  • Higher-priced items and products sold in 'Supermarket Type3' stores tend to have higher sales.

  • Conversely, Product_Allocated_Area (visibility) has a counter-intuitive relationship with sales, where lower visibility is associated with higher sales. This suggests that in-store visibility might not be a primary driver of sales for this product set, or that there are confounding factors at play.

  • The analysis also highlights the need for handling missing data in Product_Weight and Store_Size and potentially addressing the zero values in Product_Allocated_Area.

  • The multi-modal nature of Product_Price suggests that price segmentation could be a valuable feature in the model.

  • Finally, while store location and size show some influence, the type of store appears to be a more dominant factor in determining product sales.

#Plot the Store_Age using a bar graph
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
histogram_boxplot(data, "Store_Age")
plt.xticks(rotation=90)
plt.show()

<Figure size 1000x600 with 0 Axes>

  • We can clearly see that this is a multimodal distribution (not smooth bell curve)

  • we can see three main clusters of store ages:

    • A very large cluster of stores around 16 years old.
    • A smaller cluster of stores around 26-27 years old.
    • Another cluster of stores around 37 years old.

  • There are gaps in the data (with no stores with ages of 17 to 25 years, 28 and 36 years).

  • Due to the large number of stores with approximate age of 16 years, the median is also pulled there.

  • Business Insights

    • The company's history and expansion can be summarized as:
      • First Wave: A group of stores was established about 37 years ago. These are the oldest, original stores.
      • Second Wave: The company had another wave of expansion about 26-27 years ago, opening a new cluster of stores.
      • Third Wave: The most recent and largest wave of expansion occurred about 16 years ago. This is when the majority of the current stores were opened.
      • Periods of No Growth: There were long periods (as described above) where no new stores were opened, indicating pauses in the company's expansion.

Outlier Check¶

In [ ]:
# Detect outliers in all numeric columns
numeric_columns = data.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns
outliers = {}
for col in numeric_columns:
    q1 = data[col].quantile(0.25)
    q3 = data[col].quantile(0.75)
    iqr = q3 - q1
    lower_bound = q1 - 1.5 * iqr
    upper_bound = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    outliers[col] = data[(data[col] < lower_bound) | (data[col] > upper_bound)]

#remove Store_Establishment_Year and Store_Age_Years from outliers
outliers.pop("Store_Establishment_Year")
outliers.pop("Store_Age")

# Print the number of outliers in each column
#print(f"Number of outliers in {col}: {len(outliers[col])}")
#print(f"Outliers in {col}:\n{outliers[col]}\n")

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 10))

for i, variable in enumerate(outliers):
    plt.subplot(4, 4, i + 1)
    plt.boxplot(data[variable], whis=1.5)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.title(variable)

  • Weight & Price: Product_Weight and Product_MRP have relatively symmetric, though distinct, distributions. Weight is very consistent, while price is intentionally spread across wide, predefined tiers.

  • Area & Sales: Product_Allocated_Area and Product_Store_Sales_Total are both right-skewed.

  • Outliers are informative: The presence and location of outliers provide valuable insights. The skew in Product_Allocated_Area and Product_Store_Sales_Total is largely defined by these high-value outliers. The outliers in Product_MRP highlight the presence of specific value-priced items.

  • Business Insights:

    • Pricing is a Key Strategic Lever
    • Shelf Space Allocation is Not Driving Sales
    • It is important to identify and manage the "star" products. The high-revenue outliers can significantly lift a category's or store's overall performance.

Model Building¶

Define functions for Model Evaluation¶

In [ ]:
# function to compute adjusted R-squared
def adj_r2_score(predictors, targets, predictions):
    r2 = r2_score(targets, predictions)
    n = predictors.shape[0]
    k = predictors.shape[1]
    return 1 - ((1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1))


# function to compute different metrics to check performance of a regression model
def model_performance_regression(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check regression model performance

    model: regressor
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    r2 = r2_score(target, pred)  # to compute R-squared
    adjr2 = adj_r2_score(predictors, target, pred)  # to compute adjusted R-squared
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(target, pred))  # to compute RMSE
    mae = mean_absolute_error(target, pred)  # to compute MAE
    mape = mean_absolute_percentage_error(target, pred)  # to compute MAPE

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "RMSE": rmse,
            "MAE": mae,
            "R-squared": r2,
            "Adj. R-squared": adjr2,
            "MAPE": mape,
        },
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf

The ML models to be built can be any two out of the following:

  1. Decision Tree
  2. Bagging
  3. Random Forest
  4. AdaBoost
  5. Gradient Boosting
  6. XGBoost

Model Evaluation (All)¶

  • Please note that I have evaluated all the models below.
In [ ]:
#Model Evaluation Function
def evaluate_models(X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val):
    models = {
        "Decision Tree": DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
        "Bagging": BaggingRegressor(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
        "Random Forest": RandomForestRegressor(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
        "AdaBoost": AdaBoostRegressor(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
        "Gradient Boosting": GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
        "XGBoost": XGBRegressor(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, verbosity=0),
    }

    train_results = []
    val_results = []

    for name, model in models.items():
        print(f"Training {name}...")
        model.fit(X_train, y_train)

        # Training performance
        train_perf = model_performance_regression(model, X_train, y_train)
        train_perf.insert(0, "Model", name)
        train_results.append(train_perf)

        # Validation performance
        val_perf = model_performance_regression(model, X_val, y_val)
        val_perf.insert(0, "Model", name)
        val_results.append(val_perf)

    df_train = pd.concat(train_results, ignore_index=True)
    df_val = pd.concat(val_results, ignore_index=True)

    return df_train, df_val

Model Performance Observations¶

  • Based on the training and validation results above, the best model to select would be the Random Forest.

    • It has the best validation performance
      • highest R-squared (0.925)
      • highest Adjusted R-squared (0.924)
      • lowest RMSE (289.27)
      • lowest MAE (109.96)
      • lowest MAPE (0.04)
    • It outperforms all the models on every single validation metric. This indicates - High accuracy, low error and good generalization.

  • Reasonable alternative models:

    • XGBoost and Bagging: Slightly underperform Random Forest

  • Models to avoid:

    • Decision Tree: R-Squared drops in validation and indicates overfitting
    • AdaBoost: Performs poorly in both training and validation.

#Model Training & Validation Evaluation

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, RandomizedSearchCV

def evaluate_pipelines_with_search(X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, search_type="random", n_iter=10, cv=5):
    # Initialize lists to store performance results for train and val sets
    train_results_list = []
    val_results_list = []
    best_models = {}

    for name, (pipeline, param_grid) in pipelines_and_grids.items():
        print(f"\n Tuning {name}...")

        # --- Hyperparameter Search ---
        if search_type == "grid":
            search = GridSearchCV(pipeline, param_grid, cv=cv, n_jobs=-1, scoring='r2', verbose=0)
        else:
            search = RandomizedSearchCV(
                pipeline, param_grid, n_iter=n_iter, cv=cv,
                n_jobs=-1, scoring='r2', random_state=RANDOM_STATE, verbose=0
            )

        search.fit(X_train, y_train)

        #search.best_estimator_ is the best pipeline refitted on the entire X_train
        best_model = search.best_estimator_
        best_models[name] = best_model

        print(f" Best Params: {search.best_params_}")
        print(f" Best CV R-squared: {search.best_score_:.4f}")

        #Evaluate on the Training set
        print(f"  -Evaluating on training data...")
        train_perf = model_performance_regression(best_model, X_train, y_train)
        train_perf.insert(0, "Model", name)
        train_results_list.append(train_perf)

        #Evaluate on the Validation set
        print(f"  -Evaluating on validation data...")
        val_perf = model_performance_regression(best_model, X_val, y_val)
        val_perf.insert(0, "Model", name)
        val_results_list.append(val_perf)

    #Combine results into two separate DataFrames
    train_results = pd.concat(train_results_list, ignore_index=True)
    val_results = pd.concat(val_results_list, ignore_index=True)

    print("\n\n--- Evaluation Complete ---")
    return train_results, val_results, best_models

Process & Performance of tuned models¶

  1. Setup: Defining Model Pipelines and Search Grids
  • Established the pipelines_and_grids dictionary. This dictionary serves as the central control for the entire tuning operation.
  • Six models are chosen for evaluation: Decision Tree, Bagging, Random Forest, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost.
  • Each model is encapsulated within a Pipeline object that bundles two key actions:
    • Preprocessing (preprocessor): A data preprocessing step is applied first to ensure that all data (for training and cross-validation) is transformed in the exact same way (example: scaling numerical features, one-hot encoding categorical features).
    • Modeling (regressor): The specific regression model is the second step in the pipeline. This pipeline structure prevents data leakage during cross-validation and simplifies the workflow.
    • Defining Hyperparameter Search Spaces: For each model's pipeline, a corresponding "search grid" (a dictionary of parameters) is defined. These grids specify which hyperparameters to tune and what values to test.

  1. Execution: Automated Search and Cross-Validation

    • The evaluate_pipelines_with_search function acts as the execution engine. It iterates through each model defined in the pipelines_and_grids dictionary and performs the following actions:
    • Search Method: It primarily uses RandomizedSearchCV for faster sampling and just as effective for large search spaces.
    • Cross-Validation: The search for the best parameters is performed using 5-fold cross-validation (cv=5). The training data is split into 5 "folds," and the model is trained on 4 folds and validated on the 5th, repeating this process 5 times. This ensures that the performance of a given parameter set is robust and not dependent on a single train-test split.
    • Optimization Goal: The process is configured to find the parameters that maximize the R-squared (scoring='r2') score, which is the primary metric for evaluating model performance in this context.

  2. Evaluation and Model Selection

    • Identifying the Best Model: The search automatically identifies the best combination of hyperparameters based on the highest average cross-validated R² score (search.best_score_). It then refits a final model using these best parameters on the entire training dataset. This refitted pipeline is stored as best_estimator_.
    • Performance Assessment: This single best model is then evaluated on training and validation datasets:
    • Consolidated Reporting: Please see below section on model performance comparison
  • Relying on default settings provides a functional but often suboptimal baseline for performance.
  • Hyperparameter tuning, systematically customizes each model's parameters to the unique patterns in the data, which for complex models like Random Forest and XGBoost, results in a significant boost in predictive accuracy.
  • Ultimately, this optimization process is crucial for moving beyond a "good enough" model to identifying a true champion model that is robust, reliable, and delivers the best possible performance for deployment.

Model Performance Analysis and Selection

  • In our earlier results (prior to hyperparameter tuning), the following models were the top three:

    • Random Forest
    • XGBoost
    • Bagging

  • After hyperparameter tuning, we see that XGBoost has performed the best:

    • It has the best validation performance
      • highest R-squared (0.924)
      • highest Adjusted R-squared (0.923)
      • lowest RMSE (292.147)
      • second lowest MAE (126.896)
      • second lowest MAPE (0.046)

  • Tuned XGBoost outperforms all other models on multiple validation metrics.

    • Highest R-squared and Adjusted R-squared means that this model has the best overall 'fit' to the data
    • Lowest RMSE means that the model is less likely to make costly prediction errors.
    • The significant advantage of Highest R-squared and Adjusted R-squared outweighs the tiny disadvantage in MAE and MAPE.

  • Generalization and Overfitting:

    • XGBoost: R-squared drops from 0.948 to 0.924 (a drop of 0.024).
    • Bagging: R-squared drops from 0.976 to 0.917 (a drop of 0.059).
    • Random Forest: R-squared drops from 0.988 to 0.913 (a drop of 0.075).
    • The Bagging and Random Forest models show much more significant signs of overfitting than XGBoost. They performed exceptionally well on the training data but couldn't maintain that performance on the validation data. XGBoost generalizes better to unseen data, which is a sign of a more robust and reliable model.

  • Reasonable alternative models:

    • Bagging and Random Forest: Slightly underperform XGBoost

Final Choice: XGBoost

  • Highest Predictive Accuracy
  • Best at Avoiding Large Errors
  • Best Generalization

  Training XGBoost 243.878 103.795      0.948           0.948 0.038
Validation XGBoost 292.147 126.896      0.924           0.923 0.046
      Test XGBoost 293.829 129.102      0.924           0.924 0.047

Tuned XGBoost Performance on unseen Testing Data

  • Tuned Data Performance Observations:

    • The high prediction power of tuned XGBoost is seen in its R-squared value of 0.924 on unseen test data.
    • The excellent accuracy of tuned XGBoost is seen in its MAPE of 4.7% on the test data.
    • Robustness and generalization is seen in its comparable performance on test data to the validation data. The model will perform reliably and consistently on new unseen real world data.

  • Comparison to the non-tuned models:

    • The non-tuned Random Forest and XGBoost can be thought of relatively overfitting when compared to the tuned XGBoost.
    • Their training R-squared values are nearly perfect (0.990 and 0.988), which means they have essentially "memorized" the training data. The large drop in performance from training to validation (the "Overfitting Gap") is a major red flag, suggesting they would be unreliable in production.

  • The goal of tuning is not just to maximize a score, but to create a robust model that generalizes well.

  • The tuned XGBoost model has a much smaller overfitting gap (0.024). The tuning process successfully constrained the model, preventing it from memorizing the training data's noise.

  • It achieved this while maintaining a validation R-squared (0.924) that is almost identical to the overfit Random Forest model (0.925).

  • Final Conclusion and Recommendation

    • The tuned XGBoost is unequivocally the best model for deployment.

    • While the non-tuned Random Forest posted slightly better raw validation scores, it was a fragile and overfit model. The process of hyperparameter tuning transformed the XGBoost model from a similarly overfit state into a highly robust, reliable, and accurate predictor.

    • The tuned XGBoost represents the best possible balance of high performance and trustworthiness, confirmed by its excellent and consistent results on the final test set.

Observations on Serialized model recall performance

  • Actual vs Predicted Sales Observations

    • X-axis: The true, actual sales value for a product.
    • Y-axis: The sales value predicted by tuned XGBoost for that same product.
    • Red Dashed Line: This is the line of perfect prediction (where Actual Sales = Predicted Sales). The closer a point is to this line, the more accurate the prediction.
    • High Overall Accuracy:
      • The vast majority of the points are a deep blue color and are clustered very tightly around the red dashed line of perfect prediction. This is a clear visual representation of the low MAE (129) and low MAPE (4.7%) that was calculated previously. It shows the model is consistently making very good predictions.
    • Reliable Sales Prediction:
      • For actual sales values between 0 and 4,500, the points in range form a dense, narrow, dark blue band right on the perfect prediction line. This means the model is very reliable for predicting sales for the bulk of the products.

  • Business Implications & Next Steps:

    • Model Confidence: This plot should give business stakeholders high confidence in the model's predictions, especially for the majority of products in the low-to-mid sales range.
    • Large Errors Need Further Investigation: The model has flagged specific predictions where it performed poorly (the red dots). A valuable next step would be to investigate these specific data points.
      • What do these products have in common?
      • Are they from a specific Product_Type?
      • Are they sold primarily in a specific Store_Id?
      • Do they have unusual MRP values?
      • Were they part of a promotion that the model didn't have data for?
    • Improvement Potential: Answering these questions could reveal patterns that the model missed and could lead to further feature engineering to improve the model's performance on these difficult-to-predict outliers.

Deployment - Backend¶

Flask Web Framework¶

In [ ]:
%%writefile backend_files/app.py

#Importing necessary libraries
import numpy as np
import joblib  # For loading the serialized model
import pandas as pd  # For data manipulation
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify  # For creating the Flask API

#Initialize the Flask application
superkart_sales_predictor_api = Flask("SuperKart Sales Predictor")

#Load the serialized model
model = joblib.load("SuperKart_model_v1_0.joblib")


# Define a route for the home page
@superkart_sales_predictor_api.get('/')
def home():
    """
    This function handles GET requests to the root URL ('/') of the API.
    It returns a simple welcome message.
    """
    return "<center><h2>Welcome to the SuperKart Sales Predictor</center></h2>!!"

# Define an endpoint to predict churn for a single customer
@superkart_sales_predictor_api.post('/v1/predict')
def predict_sales():
    """
    This function handles POST requests to the '/v1/predict' endpoint.
    It expects a JSON payload containing property details and returns
    the predicted sales as a JSON response.
    """
    # Get JSON data from the request
    data = request.get_json()

    # Extract relevant customer features from the input data. The order of the column names matters.
    sample = {
        'Product_Weight': data['Product_Weight'],
        'Product_Sugar_Content': data['Product_Sugar_Content'],
        'Product_Allocated_Area': data['Product_Allocated_Area'],
        'Product_MRP': data['Product_MRP'],
        'Store_Size': data['Store_Size'],
        'Store_Location_City_Type': data['Store_Location_City_Type'],
        'Store_Type': data['Store_Type'],
        'Product_Id_First_Two': data['Product_Id_First_Two'],
        'Store_Age': data['Store_Age'],
        'Product_Type_Category': data['Product_Type_Category'],
        'Store_Id': data['Store_Id']
    }

    # Convert the extracted data into a Pandas DataFrame
    input_data = pd.DataFrame([sample])

    # Make a churn prediction using the trained model
    predicted_sales = model.predict(input_data).tolist()[0]

    # Return the prediction as a JSON response
    return jsonify({'Predicted Sales': predicted_sales})


# Run the Flask app in debug mode
if __name__ == '__main__':
    superkart_sales_predictor_api.run(debug=True)

Actionable Insights and Business Recommendations¶

Key Analytical Steps and Discoveries:¶

  • Data Quality: The dataset was clean with no missing or duplicate values, but has minor inconsistencies (reg vs. Regular) which were handled.
  • Feature Engineering: Three new, valuable features were created
    • Product_Id_First_Two: The product ID was reverse engineered to create high-level categories - Food (FD), Drinks(DR), Non-Consumables(NC).
    • Store_Age: Transformed the establishment year into a more usable Store_Age, revealing a "waved" expansion strategy.
    • Product_Type_Category: Product types were grouped into "Perishables" and "Non-Perishables."
  • Core Sales Drivers: The EDA and correlation analysis identified Product_MRP (price) as the single most powerful predictor of sales, followed by Product_Weight. It also dismissesed Product_Allocated_Area as a weak predictor.
  • Store Performance: The analysis revealed that:
    • OUT004 is a high-volume, "Supermarket Type2" hypermarket that drives the most total revenue.
    • OUT003 is a premium-focused "Departmental Store" that drives the highest sales per item.
    • OUT002 is a low-price, "Food Mart" format with the lowest sales.
  • Market & Customer Insights: The analysis shows a strong market preference for "Low Sugar" products and highlights the dominance of "Fruits & Vegetables" and "Snack Foods" as key revenue categories.
  • Model Selection: The modeling process identified the risk of overfitting in non-tuned models and selected the tuned XGBoost model as the best balance of high accuracy (92.4% R-squared) and reliability.
  • Deployment: The script successfully serialized the final model and set up both backend (Flask API via Docker) and frontend (Streamlit) deployment files, demonstrating a complete production-ready workflow.

Insights and Recommendations¶

The model analysis and high-accuracy predictive model choice (92.4% R-squared) have helped unlock a roadmap for SuperKart to boost revenue and optimize operations. The following data-driven recommendations will empower strategic decision-making across the business.

  1. Focus on the "Dynamic Duo": Price & Weight are key sales levers that can be tweaked
  • Insight: Product_MRP is the single most powerful driver of sales revenue.
  • Recommendation: Aggressively manage and test the tiered pricing strategy identified in our analysis (e.g., Value, Standard, Premium). Use the predictive model to forecast the revenue impact of price adjustments before implementation. Forget about increasing shelf space to drive sales—it doesn't work.
  1. Clone the "Cash Cow": Replicate the OUT004 Hypermarket Model
  • Insight: Store OUT004 is a high-volume revenue engine, generating more sales than all other stores combined. Its success is built on a massive product assortment.
  • Recommendation: Prioritize the "Supermarket Type2" format for all future expansions. Develop a "Store OUT004 Playbook" that documents its product mix and operational strategy to be replicated in other high-potential Tier 2 city locations.
  1. Ride the "Low Sugar" Health Wave: Double Down on Healthy Options
  • Insight: "Low Sugar" products are not a niche; they are a revenue powerhouse, generating more than double the sales of "Regular" sugar items.
  • Recommendation: Position SuperKart as the go-to destination for health-conscious shoppers. Increase marketing spend on the "Low Sugar" product line, expand its variety, and use the sales forecast model to ensure these high-demand items are always in stock.
  1. Supercharge Your Core Categories: Fruits, Veggies & Snacks
  • Insight: "Fruits and Vegetables" and "Snack Foods" are the undisputed top revenue-generating categories across all store formats.
  • Recommendation: Treat these categories as strategic assets. Implement targeted promotions, cross-selling initiatives, and ensure premium in-store placement to maximize their already dominant performance.
  1. Tailor Strategy to Store Type: Eliminated One-Size-Fits-All strategies

  • Insight: The stores operate on different models. OUT003 excels at selling high-value items, while OUT002 is a low-price convenience hub.

  • Recommendation: Develop distinct performance goals and inventory strategies for each store type. Benchmark OUT003 on profit margin and sales-per-item, while benchmarking OUT002 on transaction volume and basket size. Use the model created in this analysis to create store-specific sales targets that reflect their unique potential. Customize the best practices from the learnings above to create unique playbooks for each store.
